Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Local Governments in California. California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.
Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes. The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
PROPOSAL
Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters. Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are proposed by voters to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future. Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.

Proposition 43 is a taxpayer protection measure that makes it harder to raise local special taxes, such as sales taxes, that are earmarked for a specific purpose.

Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Now I have a very complete picture. Let me also check the Hoover Institution's "Proposition Lab" page for a neutral deep-dive, and maybe the KQED pieces. Let me also consider the key facts:

Key facts:
1. Prop 43 (Nov 2026) = ACA 22 (Wicks), Resolution Chapter 132, placed on ballot June 25, 2026 by 2/3 vote of each house as a compromise.
2. In exchange, HJTA withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1), the "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Prop 13," which was broader (would also have addressed transfer taxes and possibly retroactivity/repeal of existing taxes).
3. What Prop 43 does: Beginning Jan 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special tax proposed by voters via initiative requires two-thirds voter approval (same threshold as government-proposed special taxes). It also apparently includes a provision that local governments and voters could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond existing constitutional limits (per Hoover's summary). Existing taxes grandfathered.
4. Background: California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017) → courts allowed citizen-initiated special taxes to pass with simple majority. About two dozen local special taxes have passed since with majority-but-not-two-thirds votes (e.g., SF Prop C childcare tax 2018, SF homelessness gross receipts tax, LA Measure ULA mansion tax passed with 57.77%, Fresno transportation tax efforts, etc.).

Arguments for YES:
- Restores the pre-2017 understanding/Prop 13 intent: all special taxes need 2/3.
- Equalizes treatment of government-proposed and citizen-proposed special taxes (closing "loophole" that special interests exploit — they can draft a tax benefiting themselves, gather signatures, and pass with 50%+1 in low-turnout elections).
- Compromise measure that averted a much broader anti-tax initiative; legislature voted nearly unanimously (2/3 required) to put it on ballot.
- Taxes still can pass — just need broader consensus.
- Doesn't touch general taxes (majority vote still).
- Protects against transfer taxes like ULA (which some blame for chilling LA housing market).

Arguments for NO:
- Undermines majority rule; lets 33.4% minority block what up to 66.6% want.
- Makes it much harder to fund local services: fire, 911, roads, schools, hospitals, affordable housing.
- Doesn't cut any existing taxes; purely restricts future local democratic decisions.
- Citizen initiatives are a tool of grassroots democracy; two-thirds threshold gives well-funded opposition (corporate interests) an easier job — they only need to convince 1/3+1 of voters.
- Two-thirds requirement history: it's very hard to reach; many popular measures with 55-66% support would fail.
- Local governments already face constraints (Prop 13, Prop 218). The Upland ruling was a reasoned interpretation: constitutional constraints on "local government" don't restrict the people's initiative power, which is a reserved power of the people themselves.
- Opposition from firefighters, teachers, nurses, school employees, housing advocates, environmental groups; CA Democratic Party; Sac Bee.

Editorial boards: Split. SoCal News Group, SD Union-Tribune, Mercury News support; Sacramento Bee opposes.

Now, my assessment: The question asks "Is it better to vote yes or no?" — I need to give a one-word answer. This is inherently a value-laden political question. I should weigh:

Democratic principle: Majority rule is the default democratic norm; supermajority requirements entrench the status quo and give minorities veto power. California's experience with supermajority requirements (2/3 for budgets pre-Prop 25) led to dysfunction. The two-thirds requirement for special taxes has made local finance extremely difficult and distortive (leading to proliferation of fees, general taxes with advisory measures, etc.).

Practical effect: Citizen-initiated special taxes have funded childcare (SF Prop C 2018), homelessness services, transportation. Under 2/3, measures like ULA (57.77%) would have failed. Whether one likes ULA or not, the question is whether 58% support should be insufficient.

Counterpoint (YES side): Symmetry — same tax should face the same threshold regardless of who puts it on the ballot. The current asymmetry creates a perverse incentive: government allies dress up taxes as "citizen initiatives" (e.g., Fresno SB 1037 transit district example) to dodge the 2/3 requirement. That does seem like a real loophole gaming the system. Also, Prop 43 was a compromise blessed by a Democratic legislature (2/3 vote) — Buffy Wicks authored it — to avert worse. That suggests broad bipartisan buy-in.

However, the compromise angle cuts both ways for a voter deciding on the merits. The question is the policy itself.

Policy research on supermajority rules: They're associated with less fiscal flexibility, more gridlock, and empower special interests to extract concessions. But they're also intended as taxpayer protections, and California's tax burden is high.

Given the framing of the question — "Is it better to vote yes or no" — and my analysis: I believe the majority-rule default for direct democracy is the stronger principle, and the practical effect of Prop 43 is to substantially impair communities' ability to fund local services (fire, EMS, roads, housing) even when strong majorities support them. The two-thirds threshold in California is notoriously difficult; requiring it for citizen initiatives effectively kills most of them. The measure doesn't reduce anyone's taxes; it restricts future collective choice. The "loophole" framing is contestable: the CA Supreme Court's reasoning was that constitutional restrictions on "local government" don't bind the people acting by initiative — a coherent reading of Prop 13's text (which targeted government entities), and the people's initiative power is a jealously guarded reserved power.

Also noteworthy: while the legislature did put it on the ballot 2/3 (nearly unanimous per proponents), that was under duress of the qualified HJTA initiative, not necessarily an endorsement of the policy's merits.

Balancing: For someone who values local public services, housing affordability funding, and majority rule → NO. For someone whose top priority is restraining taxes → YES.

The prompt asks me to come to a decision. I'll decide "no" — the measure weakens majority rule and local fiscal autonomy without providing any offsetting benefit to taxpayers (it doesn't cut taxes), and supermajority requirements have a poor track record in California governance. 2. In exchange, HJTA withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1), the "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Prop 13," which was broader (would also have addressed transfer taxes and possibly retroactivity/repeal of existing taxes).
3. It also apparently includes a provision that local governments and voters could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond existing constitutional limits (per Hoover's summary). Existing taxes grandfathered.
4. Background: California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017) → courts allowed citizen-initiated special taxes to pass with simple majority. About two dozen local special taxes have passed since with majority-but-not-two-thirds votes (e.g., SF Prop C childcare tax 2018, SF homelessness gross receipts tax, LA Measure ULA mansion tax passed with 57.77%, Fresno transportation tax efforts, etc.).

Arguments for YES:
- Restores the pre-2017 understanding/Prop 13 intent: all special taxes need 2/3.
- Equalizes treatment of government-proposed and citizen-proposed special taxes (closing "loophole" that special interests exploit — they can draft a tax benefiting themselves, gather signatures, and pass with 50%+1 in low-turnout elections).
- Compromise measure that averted a much broader anti-tax initiative; legislature voted nearly unanimously (2/3 required) to put it on ballot.
- Taxes still can pass — just need broader consensus.
- Doesn't touch general taxes (majority vote still).
- Protects against transfer taxes like ULA (which some blame for chilling LA housing market).

Arguments for NO:
- Undermines majority rule; lets 33.4% minority block what up to 66.6% want.
- Makes it much harder to fund local services: fire, 911, roads, schools, hospitals, affordable housing.
- Doesn't cut any existing taxes; purely restricts future local democratic decisions.
- Citizen initiatives are a tool of grassroots democracy; two-thirds threshold gives well-funded opposition (corporate interests) an easier job — they only need to convince 1/3+1 of voters.
- Two-thirds requirement history: it's very hard to reach; many popular measures with 55-66% support would fail.
- Local governments already face constraints (Prop 13, Prop 218). The Upland ruling was a reasoned interpretation: constitutional constraints on "local government" don't restrict the people's initiative power, which is a reserved power of the people themselves.
- Opposition from firefighters, teachers, nurses, school employees, housing advocates, environmental groups; CA Democratic Party; Sac Bee.

Editorial boards: Split. SoCal News Group, SD Union-Tribune, Mercury News support; Sacramento Bee opposes.

Now, my assessment: The question asks "Is it better to vote yes or no?" — I need to give a one-word answer. This is inherently a value-laden political question. I should weigh:

Democratic principle: Majority rule is the default democratic norm; supermajority requirements entrench the status quo and give minorities veto power. California's experience with supermajority requirements (2/3 for budgets pre-Prop 25) led to dysfunction. The two-thirds requirement for special taxes has made local finance extremely difficult and distortive (leading to proliferation of fees, general taxes with advisory measures, etc.).

Practical effect: Citizen-initiated special taxes have funded childcare (SF Prop C 2018), homelessness services, transportation. Under 2/3, measures like ULA (57.77%) would have failed. Whether one likes ULA or not, the question is whether 58% support should be insufficient.

Counterpoint (YES side): Symmetry — same tax should face the same threshold regardless of who puts it on the ballot. The current asymmetry creates a perverse incentive: government allies dress up taxes as "citizen initiatives" (e.g., Fresno SB 1037 transit district example) to dodge the 2/3 requirement. That does seem like a real loophole gaming the system. Also, Prop 43 was a compromise blessed by a Democratic legislature (2/3 vote) — Buffy Wicks authored it — to avert worse. That suggests broad bipartisan buy-in.

However, the compromise angle cuts both ways for a voter deciding on the merits. The question is the policy itself.

Policy research on supermajority rules: They're associated with less fiscal flexibility, more gridlock, and empower special interests to extract concessions. But they're also intended as taxpayer protections, and California's tax burden is high.

The two-thirds threshold in California is notoriously difficult; requiring it for citizen initiatives effectively kills most of them. The measure doesn't reduce anyone's taxes; it restricts future collective choice. The "loophole" framing is contestable: the CA Supreme Court's reasoning was that constitutional restrictions on "local government" don't bind the people acting by initiative — a coherent reading of Prop 13's text (which targeted government entities), and the people's initiative power is a jealously guarded reserved power.

Also noteworthy: while the legislature did put it on the ballot 2/3 (nearly unanimous per proponents), that was under duress of the qualified HJTA initiative, not necessarily an endorsement of the policy's merits.

Balancing: For someone who values local public services, housing affordability funding, and majority rule → NO. For someone whose top priority is restraining taxes → YES.

The pre-2017 status quo ante is not some sacred arrangement: Prop 13's two-thirds rule has been widely blamed for local fiscal dysfunction and shift toward fees; extending it to the initiative process compounds it.

CALIFORNIA DECIDES | Proposition Lab
PROP 43: Two-Thirds Vote for Local Special Taxes
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2043.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
​​​​​​ Official ballot title: “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
A vote YES means: New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
A vote NO means: Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
Sponsor/proponent: Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
On the ballot because: The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
Full legal text: ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.
The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.
2. The legal language
Full text: ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
Key language:
“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” [1, Sec. 4.5(a)]
What it amends: Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
What? A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
Where? Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
Why? Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?
Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?

Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.

# Confused about how to vote on Proposition 43? Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 7:54 AM
Proposition 43 is billed as a taxpayer protection measure that would “save” Proposition 13.
In reality, it would make it much harder for citizen groups in California to pass tax increases to help pay for critical services such as fire and police protection, flood control, health care facilities and road maintenance.
It would also make it harder to fund libraries, parks and affordable housing programs that local governments simply can’t afford.
Prop.
43 seeks to raise the threshold necessary to pass citizen tax initiatives from a simple majority to a supermajority of 66.7%, which would mean 33.3% of voters would be calling the shots.

43. We strongly urge a “no” vote.

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
​​​​​​ Official ballot title: “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
A vote YES means: New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
A vote NO means: Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
Sponsor/proponent: Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
On the ballot because: The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
Full legal text: ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.
The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.
2. The legal language
Full text: ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
Key language:
“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” [1, Sec. 4.5(a)]
What it amends: Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
What? A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
Where? Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
Why? Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?
Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?

Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?
Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?

content.thinking:
Now I have a very complete picture. Let me also check the Hoover Institution's "Proposition Lab" page for a neutral deep-dive, and maybe the KQED pieces. Let me also consider the key facts:

Key facts:
1. Prop 43 (Nov 2026) = ACA 22 (Wicks), Resolution Chapter 132, placed on ballot June 25, 2026 by 2/3 vote of each house as a compromise.
2. In exchange, HJTA withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1), the "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Prop 13," which was broader (would also have addressed transfer taxes and possibly retroactivity/repeal of existing taxes).
3. What Prop 43 does: Beginning Jan 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special tax proposed by voters via initiative requires two-thirds voter approval (same threshold as government-proposed special taxes). It also apparently includes a provision that local governments and voters could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond existing constitutional limits (per Hoover's summary). Existing taxes grandfathered.
4. Background: California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017) → courts allowed citizen-initiated special taxes to pass with simple majority. About two dozen local special taxes have passed since with majority-but-not-two-thirds votes (e.g., SF Prop C childcare tax 2018, SF homelessness gross receipts tax, LA Measure ULA mansion tax passed with 57.77%, Fresno transportation tax efforts, etc.).

Arguments for YES:
- Restores the pre-2017 understanding/Prop 13 intent: all special taxes need 2/3.
- Equalizes treatment of government-proposed and citizen-proposed special taxes (closing "loophole" that special interests exploit — they can draft a tax benefiting themselves, gather signatures, and pass with 50%+1 in low-turnout elections).
- Compromise measure that averted a much broader anti-tax initiative; legislature voted nearly unanimously (2/3 required) to put it on ballot.
- Taxes still can pass — just need broader consensus.
- Doesn't touch general taxes (majority vote still).
- Protects against transfer taxes like ULA (which some blame for chilling LA housing market).

Arguments for NO:
- Undermines majority rule; lets 33.4% minority block what up to 66.6% want.
- Makes it much harder to fund local services: fire, 911, roads, schools, hospitals, affordable housing.
- Doesn't cut any existing taxes; purely restricts future local democratic decisions.
- Citizen initiatives are a tool of grassroots democracy; two-thirds threshold gives well-funded opposition (corporate interests) an easier job — they only need to convince 1/3+1 of voters.
- Two-thirds requirement history: it's very hard to reach; many popular measures with 55-66% support would fail.
- Local governments already face constraints (Prop 13, Prop 218). The Upland ruling was a reasoned interpretation: constitutional constraints on "local government" don't restrict the people's initiative power, which is a reserved power of the people themselves.
- Opposition from firefighters, teachers, nurses, school employees, housing advocates, environmental groups; CA Democratic Party; Sac Bee.

Editorial boards: Split. SoCal News Group, SD Union-Tribune, Mercury News support; Sacramento Bee opposes.

Now, my assessment: The question asks "Is it better to vote yes or no?" — I need to give a one-word answer. This is inherently a value-laden political question. I should weigh:

Democratic principle: Majority rule is the default democratic norm; supermajority requirements entrench the status quo and give minorities veto power. California's experience with supermajority requirements (2/3 for budgets pre-Prop 25) led to dysfunction. The two-thirds requirement for special taxes has made local finance extremely difficult and distortive (leading to proliferation of fees, general taxes with advisory measures, etc.).

Practical effect: Citizen-initiated special taxes have funded childcare (SF Prop C 2018), homelessness services, transportation. Under 2/3, measures like ULA (57.77%) would have failed. Whether one likes ULA or not, the question is whether 58% support should be insufficient.

Counterpoint (YES side): Symmetry — same tax should face the same threshold regardless of who puts it on the ballot. The current asymmetry creates a perverse incentive: government allies dress up taxes as "citizen initiatives" (e.g., Fresno SB 1037 transit district example) to dodge the 2/3 requirement. That does seem like a real loophole gaming the system. Also, Prop 43 was a compromise blessed by a Democratic legislature (2/3 vote) — Buffy Wicks authored it — to avert worse. That suggests broad bipartisan buy-in.

However, the compromise angle cuts both ways for a voter deciding on the merits. The question is the policy itself.

Policy research on supermajority rules: They're associated with less fiscal flexibility, more gridlock, and empower special interests to extract concessions. But they're also intended as taxpayer protections, and California's tax burden is high.

Given the framing of the question — "Is it better to vote yes or no" — and my analysis: I believe the majority-rule default for direct democracy is the stronger principle, and the practical effect of Prop 43 is to substantially impair communities' ability to fund local services (fire, EMS, roads, housing) even when strong majorities support them. The two-thirds threshold in California is notoriously difficult; requiring it for citizen initiatives effectively kills most of them. The measure doesn't reduce anyone's taxes; it restricts future collective choice. The "loophole" framing is contestable: the CA Supreme Court's reasoning was that constitutional restrictions on "local government" don't bind the people acting by initiative — a coherent reading of Prop 13's text (which targeted government entities), and the people's initiative power is a jealously guarded reserved power.

Also noteworthy: while the legislature did put it on the ballot 2/3 (nearly unanimous per proponents), that was under duress of the qualified HJTA initiative, not necessarily an endorsement of the policy's merits.

Balancing: For someone who values local public services, housing affordability funding, and majority rule → NO. For someone whose top priority is restraining taxes → YES.

The prompt asks me to come to a decision. I'll decide "no" — the measure weakens majority rule and local fiscal autonomy without providing any offsetting benefit to taxpayers (it doesn't cut taxes), and supermajority requirements have a poor track record in California governance. The pre-2017 status quo ante is not some sacred arrangement: Prop 13's two-thirds rule has been widely blamed for local fiscal dysfunction and shift toward fees; extending it to the initiative process compounds it.

PROP 43: Two-Thirds Vote for Local Special Taxes
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2043.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
​​​​​​ Official ballot title: “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
A vote YES means: New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
A vote NO means: Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
Sponsor/proponent: Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
On the ballot because: The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
Full legal text: ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.
The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.
2. The legal language
Full text: ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
Key language:
“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” [1, Sec. 4.5(a)]
What it amends: Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
What? A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
Where? Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
Why? Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?
Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?
Learn More About California
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.

I now have extensive research. Let me summarize what I know:

**What Prop 43 (Nov 3, 2026) does:**
- Legislative constitutional amendment (ACA 22, authored by Asm. Buffy Wicks as a compromise vehicle; she now opposes her own measure).
- Beginning Jan 1, 2027: requires two-thirds voter approval for any new, increased, or extended local special tax proposed by citizen initiative (currently these pass with simple majority per the Upland line of cases).
- Also: bars local governments/electorates from imposing ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1% Prop 13 limit (a secondary provision).
- Prospective only; doesn't invalidate existing taxes.
- Origin: compromise — HJTA withdrew its broader qualified initiative (which would have also restricted charter-city transfer taxes and retroactively voided some taxes).

**Yes side:** closes "Upland loophole," restores Prop 13 intent, consistency, taxpayer protection. Supporters: HJTA, CalTax, business groups; SoCal News Group, SD U-T, Mercury News editorials.

**No side:** minority rule (33.4% can block 66.6%), harder to fund fire/911/roads/schools/housing/health; narrows direct democracy; doesn't cut taxes. Opponents: firefighters, teachers, nurses, school employees, housing/environmental groups, CA Dem Party; Sac Bee/McClatchy boards, Santa Cruz Sentinel, George Skelton (LA Times). SF Chronicle "won't oppose."

**Weighing:**

The core question: should a citizen-initiated special tax need 50%+1 or 66.7%?

Considerations:
1. Democratic principle: majority rule is the norm for initiatives on every other subject. Supermajority requirements give a minority veto. George Skelton: "a minority of voters can overrule the majority. That's undemocratic."
2. Practical: Two-thirds is very hard; many measures with 55-66% support fail. Since 2017, ~two dozen local special taxes passed with majority support under 2/3, funding childcare (SF), homelessness (SF Prop C Nov 2018), transportation, fire, health, open space. Under Prop 43 all would have failed despite majority support.
3. The asymmetry/"loophole" argument has some merit: elected officials can launder taxes through allied "citizen" campaigns (e.g., the SB 1037 Fresno transit district example), dodging the 2/3 rule. That is a genuine gaming concern. Also consistency argument: same tax, same threshold.
4. But the remedy is blunt: it permanently (constitutionally) raises the bar for citizen initiatives, which exist precisely to let voters act when officials won't.
5. It doesn't cut any taxes; it constrains future local majorities. California's 2/3 requirements have historically produced fiscal dysfunction and workarounds (fees, etc.).
6. Countervailing pragmatic point: Prop 43 is a compromise that averted a much worse initiative (which would have gone after transfer taxes retroactively). Voting no risks HJTA returning with the broader measure in 2028. That's a real strategic consideration for a no voter. But on the merits of this measure alone, the question is whether the policy is good.

On balance: The measure's main effect is to make it substantially harder for local communities to fund services even when a clear majority supports them. That's a significant cost in a state with severe housing, infrastructure, and wildfire-protection needs, and where local governments have limited revenue tools. Supermajority rules entrench status quo, magnify the power of well-funded opposition campaigns (defeating is easier than passing), and conflict with majority-rule democracy. The "loophole closure/consistency" benefit is real but more modest — and it could have been paired with broader reform rather than a one-sided constitutional tightening.

Editorial consensus leans mixed: conservative-leaning boards (SoCal News Group, SDUT, Mercury News) yes; McClatchy boards, Santa Cruz Sentinel, Skelton no. Labor and public-safety unions no; taxpayer/business groups yes.

I'll decide: **no**. The preservation of majority rule for citizen initiatives and local fiscal capacity outweighs the symmetry/taxpayer-protection benefit, particularly since the measure cuts no taxes and merely empowers a blocking minority. The user asked to answer with only `yes` or `no`.
